content: _Vibrio_ are bacteria that naturally inhabit coastal waters, including saltwater and brackish water, which is a mixture of saltwater and freshwater often found where rivers meet the ocean. These bacteria are more prevalent from May through October when water temperatures are warmer. Among the various species of _Vibrio_, about a dozen can cause human infections collectively referred to as vibriosis. The most common species responsible for vibriosis in the United States are _Vibrio parahaemolyticus_, _Vibrio vulnificus_, and _Vibrio alginolyticus_. It is important to note that other strains of _Vibrio_ can cause cholera, but this discussion focuses on vibriosis. Vibriosis is typically contracted through the consumption of raw or undercooked shellfish, particularly oysters. It can also occur when an open wound is exposed to coastal waters. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that approximately 80,000 cases of vibriosis occur annually in the United States, with 52,000 of these cases linked to the consumption of contaminated food. The symptoms of _Vibrio_ infection vary depending on the type of exposure. Common symptoms include watery diarrhea, stomach cramps, nausea, vomiting, fever, and chills. In cases where the infection enters the bloodstream, symptoms may include fever, chills, dangerously low blood pressure, and blistering skin lesions. For wound infections caused by _Vibrio_, symptoms may include fever, redness, pain, swelling, warmth, discoloration of the skin, and discharge from the wound. Certain species of _Vibrio_, such as _Vibrio vulnificus_, can lead to severe and life-threatening complications. These infections may result in necrotizing fasciitis, a condition where the tissue around an open wound dies. While _Vibrio vulnificus_ has been referred to as flesh-eating bacteria in media reports, public health experts identify group A _Streptococcus_ as the most common cause of necrotizing fasciitis in the United States. Severe _Vibrio vulnificus_ infections often require intensive care or even limb amputation. Tragically, about 1 in 5 individuals with this infection die, sometimes within just one or two days of symptom onset. If you experience symptoms of a _Vibrio_ bloodstream or wound infection, it is critical to seek emergency medical care immediately. While anyone can contract a _Vibrio_ infection, certain medical conditions and treatments increase the risk of infection and severe complications. These include liver disease, cancer, diabetes, HIV, thalassemia, immune-suppressing therapies, medications that reduce stomach acid, and recent stomach surgery. Additionally, behaviors such as eating raw seafood (especially oysters) or exposing open wounds to coastal waters or raw seafood and its drippings can elevate the risk of infection. Diagnosis of a _Vibrio_ infection is confirmed when the bacteria are detected in a wound, blood, or stool sample. If you exhibit symptoms of infection, it is essential to inform your healthcare provider if you have recently consumed raw or undercooked seafood or if you have an open wound that may have been exposed to coastal waters or raw seafood. Treatment for _Vibrio_ infections depends on the severity of the condition. Mild infections typically do not require antibiotics and can be managed by staying hydrated to prevent dehydration caused by diarrhea or vomiting. Severe or prolonged infections, however, may necessitate antibiotic therapy. Wound infections caused by _Vibrio_ are treated with a combination of antibiotics and surgical intervention to remove dead or infected tissue. In some cases, surgery may involve amputation to prevent the spread of the infection.
